los.text: Describe the main causes, pathophysiology, clinical signs and symptoms and principles of treatment of a collapsed patient
los.html:
Immediate approach
  • DR ABC (Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation).
  • Unresponsive and not breathing normally → call cardiac arrest team (2222), start CPR 30:2, attach defibrillator.
ALS
  • Shockable (VF/pulseless VT) → shock
  • CPR 2 min
  • Adrenaline 1 mg after 3rd shock then every 3–5 min
  • Amiodarone 300 mg after 3rd shock
  • Non-shockable (PEA/asystole) → CPR + adrenaline 1 mg ASAP.
  • Treat reversible causes: 4 Hs (Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, Hypothermia) and 4 Ts (Thrombosis (coronary/PE), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins).
Collapse with output → ABCDE assessment, glucose ("DEFG: Don't Ever Forget Glucose"), ECG, bloods, VBG.
Cause groupExamplesClues
CardiacArrhythmia, MI, aortic stenosis, PE, aortic dissectionECG, chest pain, exertional
Reflex/orthostaticVasovagal, postural hypotensionProdrome, quick recovery
Hypovolaemia/shockGI bleed, ruptured AAA, ectopic, sepsis, anaphylaxisTachycardia, hypotension, melaena, back pain, rash
NeurologicalSeizure, stroke/SAH, head injuryPost-ictal confusion, focal signs, thunderclap headache
MetabolicHypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, adrenal crisisBloods, capillary glucose
ToxicAlcohol, opioids, overdosePupils, RR
OtherFalls/mechanical in elderly, frailtyCollateral history
  • Principles of treatment: resuscitate (O₂, IV access, fluids)
    • treat the cause (glucose for hypoglycaemia, naloxone for opioids, fluids/blood for bleeding, antibiotics for sepsis, adrenaline for anaphylaxis, pacing/cardioversion for arrhythmia)
    • monitor
    • collateral history
    • post-event assessment (injuries, ECG, lying/standing BP).

los.text: Describe the main causes, signs, symptoms, management and drug treatments for sepsis
los.html:
Sepsis
  • Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (Sepsis-3).
  • Septic shock: sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 despite adequate fluids (mortality >40%).
Causes
  • Chest (pneumonia, commonest), urine, abdomen (perforation, cholangitis), skin/soft tissue, lines, meningitis, endocarditis, bone/joint
  • Neutropenic sepsis.
  • Risk: extremes of age, immunosuppression, diabetes, recent surgery, indwelling devices, pregnancy.
Features
  • Fever or hypothermia, rigors, tachycardia, tachypnoea (RR ≥22: early sign), hypotension, confusion, mottled skin, oliguria, non-blanching rash (meningococcal).
  • Use NEWS2 ≥5 (or 3 in one parameter) to trigger review
  • qSOFA (RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100).
PathophysiologyPAMPs/DAMPs → widespread cytokine release → vasodilation, capillary leak, endothelial damage, microvascular thrombosis/DIC, mitochondrial dysfunction, myocardial depression → organ failure.
Sepsis Six (within 1 hour)
  • Take 3: blood cultures, lactate (VBG), urine output (catheter).
  • Give 3: O₂ (target 94–98%), IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum per local guideline, within 1 h if high risk), IV fluids (500 mL crystalloid bolus, repeat up to 30 mL/kg if hypotensive/lactate ≥4).
Then
  • Source control (drain abscess, remove infected line, surgery), escalate to ICU if persistent hypotension (vasopressors: noradrenaline), lactate not clearing
  • Review antibiotics with cultures.
Neutropenic sepsis(chemotherapy, neutrophils <0.5)Piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 h ("door to needle").

los.text: Describe the main causes, signs, symptoms, principles of management and drug treatments for anaphylaxis
los.html:
Anaphylaxis
  • Severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction
  • Rapid onset (minutes) with airway, breathing and/or circulation problems, usually with skin/mucosal changes (but these are absent in ~10–20%).
CausesFoods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, egg; children), drugs (antibiotics: penicillins; NSAIDs; anaesthetic agents/NMBs; contrast), insect venom (bees, wasps), latex, idiopathic.
Mechanism
  • Mostly type I IgE-mediated mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, PAF → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchospasm, oedema.
  • Some non-IgE (direct mast cell activation: opioids, contrast).
Features
  • A (throat/tongue swelling, hoarse voice, stridor)
  • B (wheeze, breathlessness, ↓ sats, cyanosis, respiratory arrest)
  • C (pale, clammy, tachycardia, hypotension, collapse, arrest)
  • D (anxiety, confusion, ↓ GCS)
  • E (urticaria, flushing, angioedema)
  • GI (abdominal pain, vomiting).
Management (Resus Council UK 2021)
  • Call for help, remove trigger, lie flat (sit up if breathing difficulty; don't stand).
  • IM adrenaline 1:1000 into anterolateral thigh: adult 500 μg (0.5 mL); child 6–12 yrs 300 μg; 6 months–6 yrs 150 μg; <6 months 100–150 μg. Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.
  • High-flow O₂, IV fluid bolus (500–1000 mL adult crystalloid), monitoring.
  • Refractory anaphylaxis (no improvement after 2 IM doses): IV adrenaline infusion (senior/critical care).
  • Non-sedating oral antihistamine for skin symptoms after stabilisation; steroids no longer routine (only for refractory/asthma).
  • Bronchodilators for persistent wheeze.
After
  • Mast cell tryptase (ideally at onset (after resus), 1–2 h, and >24 h)
  • Observe (≥6–12 h; biphasic reactions)
  • 2 adrenaline auto-injectors + training
  • Allergy clinic referral
  • Yellow Card for drugs
  • Document allergy.

los.text: Describe treatments used to maintain vascular function in patients presenting in emergency situations
los.html:
• First: restore volume (fluid boluses) and treat cause.
    • Vasoactive drugs are for shock persisting after adequate fluid (usually ICU/HDU, central line, arterial line).
DrugReceptorsMain effectUse
Noradrenalineα1 >> β1Vasoconstriction → ↑ SVR and MAPFirst-line vasopressor in septic shock (target MAP ≥65)
Adrenalineα1 + β1 + β2↑ HR, contractility, vasoconstriction; bronchodilationAnaphylaxis (IM), cardiac arrest (IV 1 mg), refractory shock (infusion)
VasopressinV1Vasoconstriction (non-adrenergic)Add-on in septic shock (catecholamine-sparing)
Dobutamineβ1 (>β2)Inotrope: ↑ contractility and CO; some vasodilationCardiogenic shock, low-output states
DopamineDose-dependent D1 → β1 → α1Rarely used now (arrhythmias)
Metaraminol / phenylephrineα1Vasoconstriction (reflex ↓ HR)Peripheral bolus/infusion for anaesthesia-related or temporising hypotension
MilrinonePDE3 inhibitorInodilatorCardiogenic shock
AtropineMuscarinic antagonist↑ HRSymptomatic bradycardia (500 μg IV, repeat to 3 mg)
HydrocortisoneRestores vascular responsivenessRefractory septic shock, adrenal crisis
Others in emergencies
  • IV fluids
  • Blood products
  • GTN and diuretics (acute pulmonary oedema with good BP)
  • Thrombolysis (massive PE)
  • Amiodarone/adenosine (arrhythmias)
  • Calcium gluconate (hyperkalaemia)
  • Mechanical support (intra-aortic balloon pump).
MonitoringArterial line, urine output, lactate, ECG; side effects: arrhythmias, peripheral/gut ischaemia, extravasation injury (central line preferred for noradrenaline).

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology of shock and associated compensatory mechanisms (part 2)
los.html:
Cellular level
  • ↓ O₂ delivery (DO₂ = CO × CaO₂) and/or ↓ O₂ use (mitochondrial dysfunction in sepsis: "cytopathic hypoxia")
  • → anaerobic glycolysis
  • → lactate and H⁺
  • → metabolic acidosis
  • ↓ ATP → Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure → cell swelling, ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → enzyme activation, membrane damage → cell death (necrosis/apoptosis).
MicrocirculationEndothelial activation/glycocalyx shedding → capillary leak (interstitial oedema, hypovolaemia), microthrombi (DIC), heterogeneous flow (shunting), leukocyte adhesion; ischaemia–reperfusion injury (free radicals).
Stages
1. Compensated (non-progressive)Neurohormonal reflexes maintain BP and vital organ perfusion (see part 1).
2. Progressive (decompensated)
  • Compensation fails
  • → hypotension, worsening acidosis (impairs myocardial contractility and vascular tone; ↓ catecholamine responsiveness), arteriolar dilation with venular constriction
  • → capillary pooling and fluid loss, ↓ venous return
  • → vicious cycle
  • Cardiac depression (↓ coronary perfusion, myocardial depressant factors).
3. Irreversible (refractory)Widespread cell death, multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) despite treatment.
Organ effects
  • Kidney (AKI/ATN, oliguria)
  • Lungs (ARDS: capillary leak, hypoxaemia)
  • Brain (confusion, coma)
  • Heart (ischaemia, arrhythmias)
  • Gut (ischaemia → bacterial translocation, stress ulcers)
  • Liver ("shock liver": ↑ transaminases)
  • Blood (DIC, thrombocytopenia)
  • Adrenal insufficiency
  • Hyperglycaemia.
MarkersLactate (>2 abnormal; >4 severe; clearance tracks response), base deficit, ScvO₂, urine output, mental state, capillary refill, mottling.
